title: The songs, closed
hookLine: the sisters and brothers, their forests and their freedom

lines: A WICK, A MORTAR, A LUTE.
cards: A robe sewn by hand, and someone told to sleep softly in it. A lamp's wick drawn down. A mortar, a pestle, a crooked husband, all left behind.
A flower-sweeper bowed to at sunrise. A white crane flying ahead of the storm. A lute, tuned neither too tight nor too slack.
Five weeks of the elders singing. Today, the last song of the block is the whole songbook, heard once more.

teach.b: First, the sisters. It began with the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. A nun told to sleep softly.

Punna, filling herself with good things like the moon. Mutta, so freed. Patacara watching the flame go out, then teaching women who had lost their children: you don't know where he came from or where he went.
Kisa Gotami's good friends. Ambapali's black hair. Subha, Punnika, Isidasi, Sumedha, each with her own long story, told her own way.
Second, the brothers. Then the Theragatha, the verses of the elder monks. Subhuti's hut.
The monsoon, the peacocks and the cranes. Sunita, once despised. Angulimala, the moon coming out from behind the cloud.
Kassapa's hills, Sariputta's patience, Ananda's dark directions. Third, the forests.
Again and again these songs are set outdoors: in groves, on rocky hills, in the rain, at the root of a tree. The freedom they describe isn't only inside a mind. It's in a place, with weather.
It sounds different in each mouth. For Mutta it's leaving a kitchen. For Bhaddiya it's living without fear.
For Nanda it's being pulled out of his own vanity. The collections don't flatten them into one story. They keep the names, the moods, even the complaints.
What the block leaves behind is not a doctrine stated once, but a crowd of people, women and men, saying what happened to them, in verse, for whoever would listen.

how: The Theragatha and Therigatha sit side by side in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali canon, and tradition hears in them the voices of the Buddha's early disciples.

o: chants for blessing a new monastery
the verses of the elder nuns and monks
hymns sung to the Buddha at festivals

games.q: the songs, closed: tap the pairs.
p: the verses of the elder nuns
the verses of the elder monks
a roofed hut, and rain invited

s: the elders' songs describe one single kind of freedom
freedom sounds different in each mouth: leaving a kitchen, living without fear, coming out of vanity.
the songs keep returning to the outdoors
groves, rocky hills, rain and the root of a tree run all through them.
the songs leave out the singers' complaints
they keep them: Mutta's crooked husband, Ananda's dark directions, Nanda's vanity.

games.q: you're Mutta. you've left the mortar, the pestle and your crooked husband behind. what goes into your song?
o: only lofty words: kitchens don't belong in a song.
the three crooked things you're free of, and then the deeper freedom.
nothing: a nun shouldn't sing about her old life.
games.why: Mutta names the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband, and then says she's free of the craving that leads to becoming.

practice: From all these songs, let one singer come forward without choosing, and picture where they sit: a grove, a hut, a cell with a lamp, a hillside.

Let their one line sound in you as closely as you remember it, and keep them company the way you'd sit beside an old friend who doesn't need you to talk. If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if not, just let them be near.

wordCard.voice: The songs. The verses of the elder nuns and the elder monks: forests, grief, freedom, each in its singer's own voice. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Therigatha: the verses of the elder nuns, where this block of songs began.

carryVoice: Your line: the elders sang. They sang outdoors, under trees and open sky. See you tomorrow.
